body.x: What follows is one family's story. The Rizvis are a fictional composite — no real family is described — but every step they take is a real step, in the order experienced families take them, when a proposal for their daughter Zahra arrived through a relative and a profile on Shia Rishta. Their checklist mattered less than their method: paper before feelings, questions before conclusions, and dignity kept intact even when a check failed.

The biodata arrived on a Tuesday, and the Rizvis did the hardest thing first: they read it as examiners, not as hopefuls. Names and dates were compared against the profile — spellings matched, the age was consistent, the city was the one the relative had mentioned. Zahra's father noted the claims that would need checking, in a plain list on paper: employment at a logistics firm, a degree from a named university, 'never married', and a family home in the same city. Nothing on the list was an accusation. It was simply the difference between what had been said and what had been shown, and the family agreed that no meeting would be arranged until the easy claims were easy to confirm. Zahra read the list too, and added two questions of her own at the bottom — it was, after all, her marriage being examined.
Asking around without making a noise

Verification in a close community is a delicate art: ask too loudly and you have announced a proposal that may never happen; ask too narrowly and you learn nothing. The Rizvis worked through people who owed them honesty rather than gossip — an uncle who attended the same centre as the young man's family, and a family friend who had worked in the same industry. The questions were factual and few: Does he work where he says? Is the family as described? Is there anything a father should know? The answers came back warm on character and family — and oddly vague on the job. Nobody said anything was wrong. But two people, separately, described his employment in the present tense about a role he had apparently left months earlier. The Rizvis wrote that down too, without dramatising it.
The meeting, and the question asked kindly

The families met, with Zahra present and the conversation properly hosted. Because the Rizvis had done their reading first, they could listen instead of interrogating — and they noticed that the young man spoke about his work entirely in general terms: projects, responsibilities, plans, but no employer name, no city of work, nothing that could be checked because nothing had quite been claimed. Afterwards, rather than trading suspicions, Zahra's father made one direct, courteous call to the relative who had brought the proposal: 'We liked the family. Before we go further, help us confirm his current employment — the picture is unclear to us.' The relative made enquiries. The answer, when it came, was that the young man had been out of work for most of a year and had been too ashamed to say so while the search was moving.
How a failed check was handled

This is the stage families remember, and the Rizvis were determined it would not become a story told against anyone. The refusal was given once, briefly, and without a list of charges: the families were not a match at this time, they wished him well, and the matter was closed. The biodata was not forwarded, the detail about his employment was not repeated to anyone outside the two households, and when the relative gently asked whether the door might reopen if circumstances changed, the answer was a kind no rather than a cruel never — circumstances were not the family's objection; the concealment, kindly understood, was a question they could not un-ask. Zahra's own view was sought and given weight throughout: she had liked the family, disliked being managed by half-truths, and said so plainly.
The second proposal, checked the same way

Four months later another proposal arrived — and the checks ran in the same order, producing a different texture of answers. The employer was named and confirmed by someone who had no reason to perform. The degree matched. A reference from the centre described the young man unglamorously and specifically — regular, helpful, unremarkable with money — which the Rizvis had learned to value more than praise. Where a detail was uncertain, the other family said so themselves before being asked. Verification did not create the family's confidence; it simply removed the obstacles to it. The meetings that followed could be about the real questions — temperament, plans, faith in daily life — because the factual floor had already been laid.

Notice what the Rizvis never did: they never treated verification as suspicion, never let a meeting outrun the facts, and never used a failed check as entertainment. Their method is available to any family — write the claims down, confirm the easy ones first, ask factual questions of people who owe you honesty, raise discrepancies once and directly, and close failures quietly. Whether a profile arrives through relatives, a community matchmaker or a platform like Shia Rishta — where profiles are email-verified and messaging opens only on mutual interest — the family's own checking remains the real verification. Done this way, it protects everyone's dignity, including the dignity of the person who does not marry into your family.

excerpt: Follow one family's verification journey from first biodata to a dignified no — and the careful yes that came after — to see how each check is really done.
title: How to verify a rishta profile: a Shia family's checklist
